Wave equation (utt​=c2Δu)

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Analysis Partial differential equation
OurBigBook.com Words: 23k Articles: 334
The wave equation is a second-order linear partial differential equation describing waves with finite propagation speed. In one spatial dimension its homogeneous, constant-coefficient form is
utt​=c2uxx​,c>0.
(1)
Here x is position, t is time, u(x,t) is the disturbance, and subscripts denote partial derivatives. For a wave equation on a string, u is transverse displacement; in linear acoustics, it can be a pressure perturbation. In several spatial dimensions, uxx​ becomes the Laplacian Δu. The same mathematical structure connects vibrating strings and acoustic waves, although their physical assumptions and wave speeds differ. [ref]
For the whole-line Cauchy problem, prescribe both displacement u(x,0)=f(x) and velocity ut​(x,0)=g(x). A classical solution has continuous partial derivatives through order two; f∈C2(R) and g∈C1(R) suffice for D'Alembert's formula to produce one. A finite string additionally needs boundary conditions. These statements concern the unforced model with constant c; damping, spatially varying coefficients and nonlinear terms change the solution formula.
A travelling wave F(x−ct) carries its entire profile to the right at wave speed c; G(x+ct) travels left. Their sum is again a solution by the superposition principle. A standing wave instead has a fixed mode shape whose size and sign oscillate: in sin(kx)cos(ckt), each node of a standing wave stays stationary. The distinction is especially clear in the pulse and string diagrams below. For this ideal model, the dispersion relation is ω2=c2k2: each propagation branch is nondispersive, so a localized profile translates without spreading. This makes the equation a useful reference against which to understand wave dispersion and damping.
The appealing combination is local interaction with global predictability: neighbouring displacements determine acceleration through uxx​, yet D'Alembert's formula explicitly identifies exactly which initial locations can influence a later observation. Finite propagation speed turns that observation into a domain of dependence, rather than requiring knowledge of the entire initial string.

Elastic energy of a small-slope string (u=21​Tyx2​,k=21​ρyt2​)

Words: 70
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
A string element has extra length [1+yx2​​−1]dx≃yx2​dx/2. At fixed tension T, work done supplies elastic energy density Tyx2​/2. Transverse velocity supplies kinetic-energy density ρyt2​/2. For a single travelling profile y=f(x±ct) with c2=T/ρ, the two densities agree pointwise. Their sum obeys a local energy balance with flux −Tyx​yt​. Standing waves generally exchange kinetic and elastic energy instead of maintaining equality at every instant.

Vibrating membrane

Words: 149 Articles: 2
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
A physical sheet under uniform isotropic tension per unit length T and with mass per unit area ρ has small transverse displacement satisfying ∂t2​ψ=c2∇2ψ, where c2=T/ρ. Fixed edges impose zero displacement. This mechanical membrane model neglects bending stiffness, large slopes and dissipation.

Rectangular membrane normal mode (fpq​=2c​p2/a2+q2/b2​)

Words: 106 Articles: 1
Vibrating membrane OurBigBook.com
For a rectangle of sides a and b with fixed edges, separation of variables gives ψ=Asin(pπx/a)sin(qπy/b)cos(ωt+ϕ) with positive integers p and q. Its angular frequency is ω=cπp2/a2+q2/b2​. Zero integers produce the trivial displacement, not a lower mode. The p−1 and q−1 interior nodal lines divide alternating-sign lobes.

Energy in a rectangular membrane mode (K=ρabω2A2/16)

Words: 60
Rectangular membrane normal mode OurBigBook.com
For a rectangular membrane mode with peak antinode displacement A, the integrals of each squared sine factor are half the corresponding side length. Integrating local kinetic energy density ρ(∂t​ψ)2/2 gives K=ρabω2A2sin2(ωt+ϕ)/8. The total energy is ρabω2A2/8, and potential energy has the complementary cosine-squared factor. Its time-averaged kinetic energy is ρabω2A2/16. At equal peak displacement, frequency and density, such mean energies are proportional to area.

Midpoint-plucked fixed-end string (an​=8ksin(nπ/2)/(π2n2),ωn​=cnπ/L)

Words: 106
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
A string of length L with fixed endpoints, initially displaced into a triangular tent of height k at its midpoint and released from rest, has a Fourier sine series with the coefficients in the title. Integrating the two linear halves gives an​, and symmetry cancels the even modes. Each coefficient evolves as an​cos(ωn​t) under the wave equation. The displacement vanishes everywhere at t=L/(2c), reverses sign at t=L/c, and returns after 2L/c. A straight configuration at an intermediate instant does not mean the string is at rest: its kinetic energy is then nonzero. The initial slope corner gives a finite-energy weak solution whose corner lines propagate and reflect at the ends.

Radial vibrations of a circular membrane (−(rR′)′=λrR,λ=ω2/c2)

Words: 108 Articles: 1
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
A fixed circular elastic membrane of radius a has radial normal modes satisfying the displayed Sturm-Liouville problem, with weight r, R(a)=0 and regularity at the origin. The regular solutions are Bessel functions of the first kind J0​(λ​r). Integration by parts gives the positive Rayleigh quotient λ=∫0a​r∣R′∣2dr/∫0a​r∣R∣2dr. Distinct modes are orthogonal in the weighted inner product ∫0a​rRSdr.

Power-law variational bound for a circular membrane (ν1​≤c(1+2​)/(2πa))

Words: 58
Radial vibrations of a circular membrane OurBigBook.com
For a fixed circular elastic membrane, the Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle applied to f(r)=1−(r/a)p, p>0, gives λ1​≤(p+3+2/p)/a2. The numerator of its Rayleigh quotient is p/2, and the denominator is a2p2/[2(p+1)(p+2)]. Minimization gives p=2​, λ1​≤(3+22​)/a2, and the displayed upper bound for the ordinary frequency ν1​=cλ1​​/(2π). Every p>0 has finite radial Dirichlet energy, which is the required variational admissibility condition.

Damped wave equation (utt​+αut​=c2uxx​)

Words: 162 Articles: 2
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
A wave equation with a linear damping term and positive wave speed c separates into spatial normal modes and damped harmonic oscillators. For a spatial eigenvalue k2, the time factor obeys T′′+αT′+c2k2T=0. Its characteristic roots are −α/2±α2/4−c2k2​. Thus underdamping requires ∣α∣<2c∣k∣, critical damping gives a repeated root and the second solution te−αt/2, and overdamping gives two real exponential rates. Negative α amplifies rather than damps the motion.

Fourier-mode Green function of the telegraph equation (Gk​(τ)=Θ(τ)c2e−γτsinh(dk​τ)/dk​)

Words: 102 Articles: 1
Damped wave equation OurBigBook.com
For operator c−2∂t2​+2α∂t​−∂x2​, define γ=αc2 and dk2​=γ2−c2k2. Retarded support, continuity at zero time and the derivative jump Gk′​(0+)=c2 fix the displayed normalization. Imaginary dk​ produces a damped sine; zero dk​ gives c2τe−γτ. The spatially uniform mode tends to 1/(2α) rather than decaying to zero.

Diffusion limit of the damped heat-transmission equation (D=1/(2α))

Words: 54
Fourier-mode Green function of the telegraph equation OurBigBook.com
At small wavenumber compared with αc, the slow decay rate of the damped wave operator is k2/(2α) and the other root decays on time 1/(2αc2). Long-time, long-wavelength motion therefore approaches heat diffusion with the displayed diffusivity. The original hyperbolic equation nevertheless has finite signal speed c, unlike the parabolic diffusion approximation.

Exponentially conjugated wave equation ((∂t​+γ)2u=c2uxx​,v=eγtu)

Words: 88
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
For real constants γ,c, the substitution v=eγtu turns the displayed equation into the wave equation vtt​=c2vxx​. If u(x,0)=f(x) and ut​(x,0)=g(x), then v(x,0)=f(x) and vt​(x,0)=g(x)+γf(x). For v0​=∣c∣>0, D'Alembert's formula consequently gives
u(x,t)=e−γt[2f(x−v0​t)+f(x+v0​t)​+2v0​1​∫x−v0​tx+v0​t​[g(s)+γf(s)]ds].​
(2)
The extra γf term is necessary even when the original initial velocity is zero. For c=0, take the limit to obtain u=e−γt[f+t(g+γf)]. The formula gives classical solutions for suitably smooth data and weak solutions for less regular data. Positive γ damps the transformed wave, whereas negative γ amplifies it.

Causal Fourier resolvent of a point-driven fixed string (q​n​(ω)=L2sin(kn​x0​)​kn2​−(ω−i0)2F(ω)​,kn​=nπ/L)

Words: 68
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
For ytt​−yxx​=F(t)δ(x−x0​) with zero endpoint displacement, a Fourier sine series gives qn′′​+kn2​qn​=2F(t)sin(kn​x0​)/L. With the e−iωt Fourier transform convention, the causal inverse of this oscillator uses the displayed denominator. Its inverse transform is H(t)sin(kn​t)/kn​, giving qn​(t)=2sin(kn​x0​)/(Lkn​)∫−∞t​F(s)sin[kn​(t−s)]ds when the past integral exists. The plain denominator kn2​−ω2 requires a pole prescription: its Cauchy principal value gives the time-symmetric kernel sin(kn​∣t∣)/(2kn​) instead. Homogeneous sine and cosine modes are additional freedom unless temporal data or causality are specified.

Wave speed (c)

Words: 527 Articles: 5
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
For the homogeneous one-dimensional wave equation utt​=c2uxx​ with constant c>0, wave speed means the speed at which a travelling wave profile translates. In F(x−ct), a feature initially at x=s follows x=s+ct, giving signed velocity +c; in G(x+ct) it follows x=s−ct, giving signed velocity −c. The characteristic lines for the one-dimensional wave equation therefore have slopes dx/dt=±c. The speed of either profile is c, even though the displacement at a fixed point can change sign or pass through zero.[ref]
The same c bounds the causal cone for the constant-speed wave equation. For a wave equation on a string, c=T/μ​ depends on tension and linear mass density; for small acoustic waves in stationary uniform air it is the speed of sound. This interpretation assumes the stated ideal wave equation. In media with wave dispersion, phase velocity, group velocity and the earliest signal arrival have different meanings: a measured wave crest speed need not be the speed of a wave envelope, and neither alone establishes a causal cone for the constant-speed wave equation.

Acoustic time-of-flight speed measurement (c=d/Δt)

Words: 360 Articles: 3
Wave speed OurBigBook.com
The experiment in A time of flight method to measure the speed of sound using a stereo sound card by Carlos C. Carvalho and others makes wave speed visible as a delay. Two powered microphones feed separate channels of one stereo line input. A clap beyond one end of their common axis reaches the nearer microphone first. The displayed signals show two separated onsets when enlarged; count their sample separation N to obtain Δt=N/fs​ and infer speed of sound c=d/Δt from the measured microphone spacing d. The reported sampling rate is 44100s−1. Repeating at different spacings gives a distance-versus-delay plot whose slope estimates speed of sound; dependence on distance helps identify acoustic travel rather than a fixed electronic delay. These are the paper's apparatus and observed readout, not measurements made for this article.[ref]
A controlled implementation also needs timing calibration for acoustic speed measurements. Put the microphones side by side to estimate the channel-delay offset τ0​, swap channels to check its sign, and check the acquisition clock against an independent timing reference. Measure spacings between consistent points on the microphones, keep the source outside their span and on their axis, and fit Δt=d/c+τ0​ by linear regression rather than forcing a zero intercept. Repeat pulses and compare the same onset criterion before reflections arrive. These are proposed calibration and control checks, not additional procedures claimed for the paper.
One sample corresponds to 1/fs​≃22.7μs for the reported sampling rate, so a delay of only a few samples has large relative measurement error. Background measurement noise, different microphone responses and threshold choice can move the apparent onset; reflections can supply a later competing pulse. Record temperature, keep air motion small, and compare several spacings. The result estimates speed of sound under those conditions; it cannot prove an exactly zero precursor below the instrument's sensitivity or establish finite propagation speed for every real medium. Both new diagrams in these sections show explicitly synthetic ideal wave equation solutions.[ref]

Finite propagation speed

Words: 472 Articles: 5
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
For the unforced, constant-c one-dimensional wave equation, finite propagation speed says that changing Cauchy data outside [x∗​−ct∗​,x∗​+ct∗​] cannot change the solution at (x∗​,t∗​), where c>0 and t∗​≥0. This interval is the initial-data domain of dependence. Its endpoints are found by following the two characteristic lines for the one-dimensional wave equation backwards from the observation. D'Alembert's formula makes the dependence sharper: initial displacement is sampled at the endpoints, while initial velocity is integrated over the entire interval.[ref]
For the synthetic choice c=1, (x∗​,t∗​)=(0.5,1.5) has initial-data domain of dependence [−1,2]. A change confined near x=3 is irrelevant to that observation, however large it is. If both Cauchy data vanish outside [−a,a], their compact support can influence only [−a−ct,a+ct] at t≥0. Thus an observer at x>a sees exactly zero displacement for 0≤t<(x−a)/c. There is no nonzero precursor beyond this causal cone for the constant-speed wave equation in the ideal model. This is an exact statement about the partial differential equation, stronger than an experimental failure to detect a small signal.
Support widening for the wave equation is a bound on possible influence, not a claim that every point inside the expanding interval moves. A bump function released with zero initial velocity splits into two separated travelling waves; the middle can become empty. An initial kick can instead leave an interior tail, as in the D'Alembert formula with initial velocity. Consequently finite propagation speed does not imply the Strong Huygens principle. A finite string needs boundary conditions, and the whole-line formula applies locally only until its backward causal cone for the constant-speed wave equation encounters an endpoint.

Damping

Words: 2k Articles: 16
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
Damping dissipates the energy of an oscillation, reducing its amplitude. A linearly damped string applies this mechanism to each normal mode.
Why can stronger damping make a return to equilibrium slower? A weak brake lets a spring exchange potential energy with kinetic energy many times; a very strong brake makes the final motion creep. Critical damping marks the boundary between these behaviours. The distinction depends on the force law: the classification below concerns a single damped harmonic oscillator with viscous damping, rather than every mechanism that removes energy.
Let x(t) be displacement from equilibrium, m>0 the moving mass, k>0 the spring constant, and b≥0 the constant coefficient of viscous damping. With no driving force, Newton's second law gives
mx¨+bx˙+kx=0,x(0)=x0​,x˙(0)=v0​.
(21)
The two initial conditions specify displacement and velocity. Define the undamped eigenfrequency as an angular frequency ω0​=k/m​ and the damping ratio as ζ=b/(2mk​). The ordinary differential equation becomes x¨+2ζω0​x˙+ω02​x=0. A constant weight in a vertical spring merely shifts equilibrium; it is already absorbed in the definition of x.[ref]
For example, the ideal parameters m=1kg and k=4Nm−1 give ω0​=2s−1 and critical damping at b=4kgs−1. Values b=1,4,8kgs−1 give damping ratios 0.25,1,2, respectively. These are model choices, not measured values. For release from rest with x0​>0, set X=x/x0​ and τ=ω0​t; then X′′+2ζX′+X=0, where primes now denote derivatives with respect to τ.
The left panel uses identical initial conditions X(0)=1, X′(0)=0. Underdamping produces repeated crossings of equilibrium; critical damping and overdamping give positive decreasing responses. The right panel keeps critical damping but changes initial velocity: X′(0)=−2 gives one crossing, although there is no oscillation. Both panels are exact model predictions.

Words: 338 Articles: 1
Damping OurBigBook.com
Critical damping is the repeated-root case of the viscous damping model: its two characteristic roots coincide at r=−ω0​. The solution with arbitrary initial conditions is
x(t)=[x0​+(v0​+ω0​x0​)t]e−ω0​t.
(22)
The extra factor t is essential: one exponential function alone cannot fit arbitrary initial displacement and velocity when the characteristic equation has a double polynomial root. Substitution, or taking the limit of the underdamped formula as its angular frequency tends to zero, gives the displayed expression.
The precise fastest-return statement is this: hold m, k, x0​>0 and v0​=0 fixed, and compare all ζ≥1. Every response decreases positively toward equilibrium; the critically damped response
xc​(t)=x0​(1+ω0​t)e−ω0​t
(23)
is smaller than every overdamped response at each t>0. It therefore reaches and stays within any specified band ∣x∣≤ϵx0​, 0<ϵ<1, sooner than those responses. Exact arrival at rest takes infinite time. This is a comparison among nonoscillatory regimes for these particular initial conditions, not a universal minimum of every possible settling-time criterion.
One short comparison argument uses q=∂X/∂ζ. Its initial conditions are zero and q′′+2ζq′+q=−2X′. For release from rest, X′<0 at τ>0; the causal Green function of a damped oscillator is positive at positive time for ζ≥1. Its convolution with −2X′ gives q>0: increasing damping beyond the critical value increases the remaining displacement.
There is no repeated oscillation at critical damping, but there can be overshoot once. For x0​>0, the factor in square brackets crosses zero precisely when v0​<−ω0​x0​, at
t∗​=−v0​+ω0​x0​x0​​>0.
(24)
For example, v0​=−2ω0​x0​ gives x=x0​(1−ω0​t)e−ω0​t, crossing equilibrium at t=1/ω0​ as shown above. An overdamped response can also cross once for suitable initial conditions. Conversely, specially chosen initial conditions can remove its slow exponential decay entirely. Thus the generic slow-root argument must not be applied to a response whose slow-root coefficient is zero.

With m,k>0, negative b would inject energy and lies outside the dissipative model.

The repeated-root solution also has a polynomial prefactor, so these rates alone do not describe its complete response.

Damping measurement from free decay

Words: 686 Articles: 4
Damping OurBigBook.com
An experimentally useful question is whether the disappearing oscillation follows viscous damping, and whether increasing the brake changes b rather than m or k. A published teaching protocol uses a cart on an air track, attached between two springs, with ceramic magnets providing eddy-current damping and an ultrasonic motion sensor recording position against time. Replace the magnets with equal masses in the baseline trial so the moving mass stays fixed. Obtain each spring constant from the slope of applied force versus extension, then use k=k1​+k2​. Time many baseline cycles to check ω0​≃k/m​. Compare one-magnet and two-magnet free decays; the protocol calls for a fit of the full trace including its offset. [ref]
The following additional controls make the inference testable. Level the air track and hold its air supply fixed. Check the ultrasonic motion sensor at several stationary flag positions against a ruler, including the full planned travel range; record the offset and scale correction. Check elapsed acquisition time against an independent clock, and choose a sampling rate that resolves many samples within the shortest expected oscillation period. Record the resting equilibrium before and after each run. Release the cart from a small measured displacement with minimal initial velocity, with the driving apparatus inactive. Repeat at several release sizes and magnet settings while keeping the springs and total mass unchanged. These are proposed calibration and repeatability checks, not reported measurements from the source.
For underdamping, fit the recorded position to y(t)=yeq​+Ae−αtcos(ωd​t+ϕ) by nonlinear regression. The readout to inspect is a sequence of alternating extrema about yeq​ with shrinking amplitudes, and the deviations of the fitted curve from the recorded points. The model predicts
α=2mb​=ζω0​,α2+ωd2​=mk​.
(31)
Compare the right-hand side, determined independently from mass and spring constants, with the fitted left-hand side. A good fit supports a constant-coefficient single normal mode over the observed range; it does not establish a universal microscopic force law. The published protocol denotes the decay rate by b and the velocity-proportional coefficient by c; here they are α and b, respectively.
At critical damping or overdamping, fit the corresponding nonoscillatory response including its offset and both initial conditions, rather than forcing a damped cosine onto the data. Adjusting the brake can explore the transition, but the cited protocol does not establish that its one-magnet or two-magnet settings attain critical damping. A near-critical trace over a short interval can be hard to distinguish from neighbouring damping ratios.
Important limitations are finite sensor range, missed or reflected acoustic wave pulses, measurement noise near equilibrium, nonzero release velocity, and position-dependent magnetic braking. Changing the release size tests for quadratic drag or nonlinear spring response; inspecting deviations near turning points can expose kinetic friction. Slow drift of the offset can imitate a long overdamped tail. Report uncertainties in fitted rates and independently measured m,k; absence of a visible crossing only bounds the behaviour within the instrument's sensitivity and recording interval. No numerical experimental results are asserted here.

Normal mode

Words: 3k Articles: 35
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
A normal mode, also called an eigenmode, is a pattern of free oscillation in a linear system whose relative displacements stay fixed while a single temporal factor changes their size and sign. For an undamped stable vibrational mode,
u(x,t)=ϕ(x)q(t),q(t)=Acos(ωt+φ).
(46)
Here ϕ is the mode shape, A sets the amplitude, ω is the eigenfrequency expressed as an angular frequency, and φ is the oscillation phase. Every snapshot is a scalar multiple of the same mode shape; neighbouring regions may move in opposite directions. Normal modes of a double pendulum show that normal modes also describe coupled discrete systems, beyond strings. Their shapes are eigenvectors, rather than spatial eigenfunctions. [ref]
For the ideal wave equation on a string, take a uniform string of length L with constant tension τ and linear mass density μ. Assume small transverse slope, negligible bending stiffness, no damping, and fixed endpoints. Its wave speed is c=τ/μ​, and the nonzero normal modes are
un​(x,t)=Asin(Lnπx​)cos(ωn​t+φ),ωn​=Lnπc​,fn​=2πωn​​=2Lnc​,n=1,2,3,….
(47)
The angular frequency ωn​ is in radians per second; the frequency fn​ is in hertz. The wavelength is 2L/n. The mode shape has n loops separated by nodes of a standing wave, including both fixed endpoints. [ref]
As a worked example, choose L=1m, τ=1N, and μ=1kgm−1. Then c=1ms−1 and f1​=0.5Hz, f2​=1Hz, f3​=1.5Hz. Their oscillation periods are T1​=2s, T2​=1s, and T3​=2/3s. These are deliberately simple model parameters, rather than measurements of a musical instrument. The plot divides displacement by A so that the three mode shapes can be compared, and uses each mode's own oscillation period for its snapshots.
For φ=0, at t=Tn​/4 every point has zero displacement, but most points have nonzero velocity. Only zeros of the mode shape are permanent nodes of a standing wave. At t=Tn​/2 the original mode shape has reversed sign, and at t=Tn​ it returns. The synchronized conversion between kinetic energy and potential energy is shown in normal-mode energy exchange.
The short derivation uses separation of variables: substituting u=ϕq into the wave equation gives ϕ′′+k2ϕ=0 and q′′+c2k2q=0. The fixed-end boundary conditions remove the cosine spatial term and require sin(kL)=0, hence k=nπ/L and ωn​=ck. Different geometries and boundary conditions give different eigenfunctions; a sine mode shape is a property of this uniform fixed string, not a universal form of an eigenmode.
The usefulness is that a complicated vibration becomes a collection of harmonic oscillators. For sufficiently regular fixed-end initial data, the Fourier sine series gives
u(x,t)=∑n=1∞​sin(Lnπx​)[an​cos(ωn​t)+bn​sin(ωn​t)].
(48)
The initial displacement and velocity determine an​ and bn​. This is the superposition principle in a Fourier sine basis, and modal energy distribution measures how strongly each normal mode is excited. The striking simplification is that each component keeps its identity while their sum can continually change shape. [ref]
These independent normal modes belong to the linear model. At larger slopes, changing tension introduces nonlinear effects and can couple the modes. A linearly damped string still admits a Fourier sine basis, but its temporal factors decay and need not oscillate; its energy dissipation identity for a linearly damped string replaces conservation of energy. More general damping need not leave undamped mode shapes independent.

The first term evolves displacement released from rest; the second evolves initial velocity. The factor 1/(2c) converts an integral of velocity over distance into displacement. On a finite string the formula applies before the backward characteristic curves reach an endpoint, or globally after an extension that enforces the boundary conditions. [ref]
For a completely smooth example, choose a bump function with compact support:
b(z)={exp(1−1−z21​),0,​∣z∣<1,∣z∣≥1,​f(x)=Ab(x/a),g(x)=0,
(59)
where a>0 sets the half-width and A sets the initial peak. Then

Zero initial velocity forces equal left and right contributions; a purely right-moving initial profile instead requires g=−cf′. Thus “released from rest” and “launched to the right” describe different Cauchy data.
The domain of dependence of (x∗​,t∗​), for t∗​≥0, is contained in [x∗​−ct∗​,x∗​+ct∗​] on the initial line. More precisely, displacement contributes only through the two endpoints, while initial velocity contributes throughout the interval. With c=1, x∗​=0.5 and t∗​=1.5, that interval is [−1,2]. Changing either initial datum outside it cannot change u(0.5,1.5). If both initial data vanish outside [−a,a], the solution vanishes outside [−a−ct,a+ct]: this is finite propagation speed. The expanding interval bounds possible influence; it need not be filled by nonzero displacement, as the separated bumps demonstrate.
Historically, d'Alembert studied the vibrating-string problem in “Recherches sur la courbe que forme une corde tendue mise en vibration”, in the Berlin Academy's volume for the year 1747, pages 214–219. The memoir introduces the differential equation and integrates it through two arbitrary one-variable functions. The original geometric problem makes the formula's enduring appeal clear: arbitrary initial shapes can be handled without first decomposing them into normal modes. [ref]
For a brief derivation, use characteristic coordinates ξ=x−ct and η=x+ct. The chain rule gives utt​−c2uxx​=−4c2uξη​, so u=F(ξ)+G(η). The initial conditions yield F+G=f and −cF′+cG′=g. Integrating these relations gives the displayed formula; the arbitrary integration constants cancel in their sum.

A wavenumber measures how rapidly a wave phase changes with distance. Two conventions coexist: angular wavenumber counts radians per unit length, while ordinary spatial frequency counts cycles per unit length. For a monochromatic wave with wavelength λ>0,
K=λ2π​,νx​=λ1​,K=2πνx​.
(64)
Here K≥0 is the magnitude of the angular wavenumber. The symbol k can instead denote a signed one-dimensional angular wavenumber: a factor eikx has wavelength 2π/∣k∣ for real k=0. Both conventions have dimensions of inverse length; writing radm−1 or “cycles per metre” exposes the convention. A quoted value in m−1 alone does not resolve the factor of 2π. Spectroscopic wavenumber usually uses the cycles-per-length convention.[ref]
For a real monochromatic plane wave, fix the convention
u(x,t)=Acosϕ(x,t),ϕ=k⋅x−ωt+ϕ0​,K=∣k∣.
(65)
The wavevector k supplies both the spatial wave phase slope and the normal to the wavefronts; its dot product with position makes the wave phase constant on parallel planes. The angular frequency is ω=2πf, with f>0 the ordinary frequency. Moving a distance λ along k changes the wave phase by 2π. Holding a wave crest's wave phase fixed gives its phase velocity ωk/K2 and phase speed
vp​=Kω​=fλ.
(66)
In one dimension the signed phase velocity is ω/k. This identifies a moving pattern; it does not identify the motion of the medium's particles or a wave packet's group velocity.
For the synthetic plane wave below, choose λ=0.40m and f=5Hz. Then K=5πradm−1, νx​=2.5 cycles per metre, ω=10πrads−1, and vp​=2ms−1. The wave crests are 0.40m apart at one instant; after a quarter oscillation period, each has advanced 0.10m. The lower panel retains whole turns of wave phase, making its slope visible instead of reducing it modulo 2π.

The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem states the precise reconstruction conditions for a bandlimited function; a finite scan introduces further limitations.

Au(x)​=cos(2πν1​x)+21​cos(2πν2​x),ν1​=2m−1,ν2​=8m−1,

Wavelength (λ)

Words: 1k Articles: 15
Wavenumber OurBigBook.com
The wavelength λ is the spatial period of a monochromatic wave, measured at a fixed time along the wavevector. For a plane wave with a sinusoid as its profile, it is the distance between consecutive wave crests, or between any consecutive points with the same wave phase modulo 2π:
λ=∣k∣2π​=fvp​​.
(69)
Here k uses angular wavenumber, f is ordinary frequency, and vp​ is phase speed. A distance between arbitrary zero crossings need not be a wavelength: consecutive zeros of a sinusoid are only λ/2 apart, with opposite slopes. In a standing wave, consecutive nodes of a standing wave are also λ/2 apart; λ refers to the constituent travelling waves, even though the nodes of a standing wave do not travel.
Across a stationary interface between stationary linear media, the incident, reflected and transmitted monochromatic waves have the same frequency. The boundary conditions must hold at every time: terms oscillating with different angular frequencies cannot cancel throughout the entire time record. Each medium's dispersion relation then determines its own angular wavenumber and wavelength, so
f1​=f2​,λ1​λ2​​=vp,1​vp,2​​.
(70)
For electromagnetic radiation in a transparent medium with refractive index n, vp​=c0​/n and λ=λ0​/n, where c0​ is the vacuum speed of light. A synthetic example with λ0​=600nm and n=1.5 gives λ=400nm at the same frequency. This conservation argument assumes time-independent linear material response and a stationary interface in the chosen frame. A moving interface can produce a Doppler effect; time-dependent or nonlinear response can change or generate frequencies.[ref]
A broad frequency spectrum generally supplies many component wavelengths, rather than one wavelength for an entire pulse. Even two tones have both their individual wavelengths and a different overall repetition distance: the 2- and 8-cycle-per-metre sum in spatial sampling of a wave repeats after 0.50m, but contains the finer 0.125m structure. A narrow wave packet can have an approximate carrier wavelength; the wave envelope propagates approximately at group velocity, determined by the slope of the dispersion relation. Substituting that group velocity into λ=vp​/f generally gives the wrong carrier wavelength. Where the medium varies slowly, local wavelength gives a more useful description.

Acoustic wavelength measurement (λ=2d)

Words: 1k Articles: 13
Wavelength OurBigBook.com
An acoustic wavelength measurement makes an invisible spatial pattern readable with a ruler. The authored guide Interesting and inexpensive experiments for high school physics by Joe Wolfe places a loudspeaker near a pipe's open end, drives it with an oscillator, and slides a microphone attached to a metre rule through the pipe. An oscilloscope or computer displays the microphone signal. Its oscillation amplitude rises and falls with position; adjacent minima locate pressure nodes of a standing wave a distance d=λ/2 apart. A cap gives a pressure antinode at the closed end; an open end has a pressure node just outside it. These are pressure patterns, distinct from displacement patterns. The guide advises wavelengths longer than the pipe diameter, sufficient pipe length to locate both a node and an antinode, and frequency spectrum analysis to distinguish the intended tone from other sounds.[ref]
The inference follows from superposition of two oppositely directed acoustic plane waves. In an ideal uniform, lossless pipe, taking equal pressure amplitudes P and a rigid cap at x=0 gives
p′(x,t)=Pcos(kx−ωt)+Pcos(kx+ωt)=2Pcos(kx)cos(ωt).
(71)
The time-varying pressure perturbation p′ has local oscillation amplitude 2∣Pcos(kx)∣. Its zeros are separated by π/∣k∣=λ/2. Unequal incident and reflected amplitudes leave nonzero minima, but their spacing remains λ/2 in this ideal model. A microphone detects that pressure variation through a changing electrical signal, rather than watching a wave crest move. Record the tone's frequency too, then infer phase speed vp​=2fd.
For proposed controls, keep the drive frequency and amplitude fixed during a scan, verify the frequency on the recorded signal, and repeat the scan in both directions. Fit several minimum positions xj​=a+jd using linear regression to reduce dependence on one pair of positions. Check the ruler scale and use one consistent reference point on the microphone. Compare with the source switched off to locate background measurement noise; use frequency spectrum analysis to check for additional tones, and reduce drive if the trace ceases to resemble a sinusoid. Record air temperature and avoid strong air motion. These are suggested controls, not additional procedures or observations attributed to the guide.
The pipe must support approximately plane waves over the measured region: transverse structure at shorter wavelengths, the microphone's finite size, and disturbance by the ruler can compromise the interpretation. Weak reflection gives shallow minima, while damping and other reflections can shift the extrema of the simple two-wave model. Measure interior spacings rather than assuming the first minimum is exactly at the pipe lip. A short scan may not include enough minima to estimate d reliably, and drift during sequential scanning can imitate spatial variation.
For an explicitly hypothetical calculation, f=1000Hz and d=0.1715m give λ=0.3430m, K≃18.3183radm−1, and vp​=343.0ms−1. No such measurements are claimed here. If independent small measurement errors in f and fitted d have standard deviations σf​ and σd​, first-order error propagation gives σvp​​/vp​≃(σf​/f)2+(σd​/d)2​. A systematic scale error or changing air conditions requires separate assessment.

For z=R2+X2​ with reactance X=ωL, linear differentiation gives dz=(RdR+XdX)/z. Independent standard uncertainties give the title formula; correlated inputs add 2RXCov(R,X)/z2. Hard error bounds instead add absolute linear contributions. The meaning of an error bar is an additional measurement assumption, not a consequence of the impedance formula.
Refractive-index uncertainty from Snell's law (σn2​/n2=cot2iσi2​+cot2rσr2​−2coticotrCov(i,r))
Words: 55
Propagation of uncertainty OurBigBook.com
For air approximated by index one, n=sini/sinr, so dn/n=cotidi−cotrdr. Taking the variance gives the displayed first-order error formula, with angles and their errors in radians. Independence removes the covariance term; hard error bounds require a different combination rule. Common angular-zero errors can produce covariance and should not automatically be added in quadrature.
Moment-of-inertia uncertainty for an annulus
Words: 36
Propagation of uncertainty OurBigBook.com
For axial moment of inertia I=m(a2+b2)/2, linear sensitivity to mass and outer/inner radius is dI=(a2+b2)dm/2+mada+mbdb. Independent standard uncertainties give σI2​=[(a2+b2)σm​/2]2+(maσa​)2+(mbσb​)2. Correlated measurements instead require the full covariance quadratic form. For deterministic bounds, add the absolute linear contributions rather than their squares.
Uncertainty in a cosine of a measured angle (σS2​=cos2(qθ)σA2​+[qAsin(qθ)]2σθ2​)
Words: 40
Propagation of uncertainty OurBigBook.com
For S=Acos(qθ) with independent standard uncertainties, linear propagation gives σS2​=cos2(qθ)σA2​+[qAsin(qθ)]2σθ2​. Angular uncertainty must be in radians when using this derivative. Covariance adds cross terms for correlated inputs. Strict error bounds instead add absolute first-order contributions; they do not justify Gaussian significance tests.
Monomial uncertainty propagation (σf2​/f2≃∑ij​ai​aj​Cov(xi​,xj​)/(xi​xj​))
Words: 122 Articles: 1
Propagation of uncertainty OurBigBook.com
For positive measured inputs and f=C∏i​xiai​​, logarithmic differentiation gives df/f=∑i​ai​dxi​/xi​. Applying propagation of uncertainty yields the displayed covariance formula. For independent input errors it reduces to σf​/∣f∣≃[∑i​(ai​σi​/xi​)2]1/2. If the input uncertainties are strict bounds rather than standard deviations, a first-order conservative bound is ∣Δf∣/∣f∣≲∑i​∣ai​∣Δxi​/∣xi​∣. These are different statistical interpretations; a product formula alone does not choose between them.
Mass ratio from spring oscillation frequencies (m1​/m2​=(ν2​/ν1​)2)
Words: 64
Monomial uncertainty propagation OurBigBook.com
For the same massless spring obeying Hooke's law, the frequency is ν=(2π)−1k/m​. The displayed mass ratio follows. For small independent frequency errors with common fractional standard uncertainty ϵ, monomial uncertainty propagation gives σR​/R≃8​ϵ. If ϵ instead describes individual measurements and each sample mean uses n independent trials, its standard error is smaller by n​, giving σR​/R≃8/n​ϵ. Four times as many trials halve this statistical uncertainty; a common calibration error needs its covariance included.
Repeated-timing uncertainty in a pendulum gravity measurement (σg2​/g2=(σL​/L)2+4σT2​/(NT2))
Words: 65
Propagation of uncertainty OurBigBook.com
For simple pendulum oscillation period T in the small-angle approximation, g=4π2L/T2. If the length measurement and N identically precise timing measurements have independent errors, the timing sample mean has standard error σT​/N​. Propagation of uncertainty gives the title formula. A target fractional standard uncertainty ϵ requires N≥4(σT​/T)2/[ϵ2−(σL​/L)2], rounded upward to an integer. No amount of repeated timing can beat the floor σL​/L without improving the length measurement; correlated errors or a timing systematic error require a different model.

Local wavelength (λloc​=2π/∣∇ϕ∣)

Words: 134
Wavelength OurBigBook.com
For a locally oscillatory wave written u(x,t)=A(x,t)cosϕ(x,t), the local wavevector is kloc​=∇ϕ, where ∇ is the spatial gradient. The local wavelength 2π/∣kloc​∣ measures local wave phase spacing normal to the wavefront. Interpreting it as a crest separation requires the amplitude and local wavevector to vary little over one wavelength, as in the WKB approximation. Along a unit direction e the corresponding local repeat distance is 2π/∣kloc​⋅e∣, if that dot product is nonzero; oblique sampling measures this projected spacing.
A real snapshot alone does not uniquely specify A and ϕ: their meaning requires a chosen oscillatory component or physical approximation. Strong interference, zeros of amplitude, and rapidly changing media can defeat a single-carrier description. If ∇ϕ=0, the local reciprocal formula gives no finite wavelength; it does not establish an exact global spatial period.

Klein-Gordon equation

Words: 639 Articles: 12
Wave equation OurBigBook.com
The one-dimensional Klein-Gordon equation
ϕtt​−c2ϕxx​+A2c2ϕ=0
(72)
has positive-frequency dispersion relation ω(k)=ck2+A2​.

Two coupled real Klein-Gordon fields (m±2​=m2∓g)

Words: 85 Articles: 1
Klein-Gordon equation OurBigBook.com
For interaction density gϕ1​ϕ2​, the combinations ϕ±​=ϕ1​±ϕ2​ diagonalize the equations into independent Klein-Gordon equations with the displayed mass squares. When 0<g<m2, all Fourier frequencies are real and nonzero. Initial data in one original field generally excite both normal combinations.

Field-amplitude beating of coupled Klein-Gordon modes

Words: 51
Two coupled real Klein-Gordon fields OurBigBook.com
A single spatial Fourier pattern initially displaced in one field excites two different normal frequencies. Their sum and difference generate slowly varying amplitude envelopes in the original fields. Total coupled-field energy is conserved, but the separate uncoupled energies need not be, and zeros of one displacement envelope do not automatically imply exact complete energy transfer.

Klein paradox

Words: 179 Articles: 2
Klein-Gordon equation OurBigBook.com
In a sufficiently strong electrostatic step, the positive-energy incident channel overlaps a negative-kinetic-energy channel on the far side. For a charged scalar field the outgoing antiparticle branch has negative charge current, allowing reflected particle current larger than the incident current while signed charge is conserved. The external source supplies energy for particle-antiparticle creation. This requires a multiparticle interpretation; negative transmitted charge current is not a negative probability.

Klein-Gordon step amplification (R=(k+Q)2/(k−Q)2,T=−4kQ/(k−Q)2)

Words: 61
Klein paradox OurBigBook.com
For the outgoing negative-energy branch q=−Q, matching the field and its spatial derivative gives these signed charge-current ratios. Their sum is one although reflection exceeds one. The ideal sharp step has a singular stationary matching denominator at E=V0​/2 in the supercritical range. It is not a finite single-particle probability prediction; wavepackets, source preparation and field quantization matter for its physical interpretation.

Outgoing analytic branch of Klein-Gordon step momentum (q(z)=z−mc2​z+mc2​/(ℏc))

Words: 55
Klein paradox OurBigBook.com
Set z=E−V0​+i0 and continue both roots from the upper half-plane. The right-hand wavenumber is positive above the positive-energy threshold, positive imaginary inside the gap, and negative below the negative-energy threshold. Its group velocity in the last region remains rightward because both momentum and kinetic energy are negative. Choosing a positive real root there instead specifies an incoming wavepacket from the right.

Nonlinear Klein-Gordon equation (∂t2​ϕ−∂x2​ϕ=f(ϕ))

Words: 107 Articles: 1
Klein-Gordon equation OurBigBook.com
A local scalar nonlinearity preserves Lorentz covariance of the wave operator when the wave speed is one. If f=F′, the equation follows from L=(∂t​ϕ)2/2−(∂x​ϕ)2/2+F(ϕ). The physical potential is −F, so its sign must be distinguished from the sign written in the Lagrangian.

Power-law nonlinear Klein-Gordon pulse (w=Csech2/(n−1)(Bx))

Words: 64
Nonlinear Klein-Gordon equation OurBigBook.com
For f(w)=−aw+bwn, with a,b>0 and integer n>1, a positive localized static pulse has Cn−1=a(n+1)/(2b) and B=(n−1)a​/2. Writing the same profile as [Acosh2(Bx)]1/(1−n) instead gives A=2b/[a(n+1)]. These are different amplitude conventions for the same solution. A Lorentz boost moves the pulse at speed tanhβ, preserves its peak height and contracts its width by 1/coshβ. Existence alone does not imply dynamical stability.

Homogeneous massive-scalar equation in an expanding universe (ϕ¨​+3Hϕ˙​+m2ϕ=0)

Words: 52
Klein-Gordon equation OurBigBook.com
A canonical spatially homogeneous field with V=m2ϕ2/2 obeys ϕ¨​+3Hϕ˙​+m2ϕ=0. The 3Hϕ˙​ term expresses dilution of field momentum by expansion. Conservation of its stress energy gives this equation wherever ϕ˙​=0; the canonical field equation is needed to fix an identically stationary interval, while continuity extends a regular solution across isolated turning points.

Real bounded Fourier modes of the Klein-Gordon equation

Words: 80
Klein-Gordon equation OurBigBook.com
With inverse-time convention eiωt, the half-line Klein-Gordon equation σtt​−σrr​+μ2σ=0 has spatial normal modes Aeikr+Be−ikr, where k=ω2−μ2​>0 above threshold and k=iμ2−ω2​ below it. For the branch even in ω, reality above threshold requires A(ω)=B(−ω)∗. Below threshold boundedness eliminates B, and reality requires A(ω)=A(−ω)∗. At threshold the spatial differential equation instead has the basis 1,r; boundedness retains only the constant mode. A spectral integral with ordinary integrable functions as amplitudes ignores the isolated threshold points, while distribution amplitudes can represent the surviving monochromatic constant-spatial modes.

Exponential initial-velocity tail for the Klein-Gordon equation (u(x,t)=te−∣x∣(∣x∣>t))

Words: 63
Klein-Gordon equation OurBigBook.com
For utt​=uxx​−u with u(x,0)=0 and ut​(x,0)=e−∣x∣, the solution outside ∣x∣≤t is exactly te−∣x∣. On the positive half-line, te−x satisfies both the equation and initial data; the finite propagation speed limits dependence at x>t to positive initial points. Uniqueness on this domain of dependence proves the formula there, and reflection gives the negative half-line. The exterior tail is nonzero because the initial velocity is not compactly supported.

Stationary-phase asymptotic of a Klein-Gordon wave along a subluminal ray

Words: 62 Articles: 1
Klein-Gordon equation OurBigBook.com
For zero initial velocity and Fourier amplitude a(k), observation along x=Vt with 0≤V<c selects the two stationary wavenumbers ±k0​, where
k0​=c2−V2​AV​.
(73)
Writing s=c2−V2​, the leading oscillation has angular frequency As and amplitude proportional to t−1/2.

Upward zero crossings of an oscillatory stationary-phase tail

Words: 21
Stationary-phase asymptotic of a Klein-Gordon wave along a subluminal ray OurBigBook.com
If the leading asymptotic is Ct−1/2cos(Ωt+γ) with C>0, its upward zero crossings satisfy
Ωt+γ=23π​+2πn
(74)
to leading order.
